name: Operational Model
one_liner: The infrastructure side of the architecture: nodes, deployment units, connections.
purpose: The Operational Model describes the 'operational' aspect of an IT system's architecture, focusing on the system's infrastructure from both a logical and a physical perspective. It describes the required operational characteristics and the network of computer systems, peripherals, software, middleware and application software that support the system's users, including the operational distribution into deployment units, the nodes, their placement across locations and the connections between them. For systems hosted in a third party's data centre it is a key input for proper support and maintenance.

fields.what: Describes the operational aspect of the IT system's architecture — the infrastructure, logically and physically.
fields.pollux: Four environments — development, test, pre-production and production — with the replica load in each.

fields.what: The required operational characteristics the infrastructure must deliver to meet functional and non-functional requirements.
fields.pollux: Nightly load must complete before 06:00 CET so the quarter-end pack can be assembled in one day.

fields.what: The architecture's network of computer systems and associated peripherals supporting the system's users.
fields.pollux: Application and database nodes in the Kirchberg data centre, with a warm standby.

fields.what: Systems software, middleware and application software required to support the users of the system.
fields.pollux: Container runtime, message broker for the delta load, and the reporting API service.

fields.what: The operational distribution — the system's components grouped into deployment units that are deployed together.
fields.pollux: Three units: data layer, API plus reconciliation service, portal UI.

fields.what: The nodes, and the placement of nodes and users across locations — where each part physically runs.
fields.pollux: Internal users at Kirchberg; national-authority users reach a separate external access node.

fields.what: The connections needed to support the required interactions between components and meet the requirements.
fields.pollux: One-way link from the lending platform to the replica; no path back into CASTOR.

fields.what: Organisation standards and policies that affect infrastructure design — security, document management, data protection.
fields.pollux: External access zone separated from internal networks after Brandeis and Turing reviewed it.

fields.what: Check the Business Case and Project Charter so the project context and proposed solution are understood before designing infrastructure.
fields.pollux: National-authority access was a charter need (N4), so the access zone is planned from the start.

fields.what: Several UML models, deployment diagrams in particular, because infrastructure can be seen from different perspectives.
fields.pollux: One deployment diagram per environment, kept beside the Architecture Overview component diagram.

fields.what: Manage the system's operational complexity and ensure it is viable at both development and operational stage.
fields.pollux: Standby node dropped from Release 1 scope after operations judged the failover unmaintainable.

fields.what: Keeping the two aligned is why feasibility is manageable at all — the guide calls this an important activity.
fields.pollux: Einstein reviews both artefacts together at every release boundary.

fields.what: Refined as the project evolves, to detail the required operational characteristics as understanding improves.
fields.pollux: Updated for Release 3 when the external access zone became real infrastructure.

fields.what: Where the system is hosted in a third party's data centre it is a key input for support and maintenance.
fields.who: PM opens the channel to hosting services
fields.pollux: Hosting stays in-house at Kirchberg; the model is still the handover document to operations.

fields.what: The whole A-PCT contributes and the broader stakeholder community is informed of crucial operational decisions.

It is created in Initiating, not Planning — it is an IT governance artefact.
It is not the PM² Transition Plan: no training, no business readiness here.
